prompt: Planet X orbits a star at four times the orbital radius of planet Y. What is $\dfrac{T_X}{T_Y}$?
markscheme: **C.** Kepler's third law: $T^{2}\propto r^{3}$, so $T\propto r^{3/2}=4^{3/2}=8$.

prompt: State Kepler's second law and use it to explain where a comet on an elliptical orbit moves fastest.
markscheme: The line joining a planet (or comet) to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times **(A1)**; to sweep the same area when close to the Sun the comet must move faster, so it is fastest at its closest approach (perihelion) **(R1)**

prompt: Calculate the gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon. $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$; Earth: mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m. Moon mass $7.35\times10^{22}$ kg; Earth–Moon distance $3.84\times10^{8}$ m.

concept: Treating extended bodies as point masses
prompt: State two situations in which an extended body can be treated as a point mass when calculating gravitational forces.
markscheme: When the body is spherically symmetric (outside it, it acts as if all its mass were at its centre) **(A1)**; when the separation is very large compared with the sizes of the bodies **(A1)**

prompt:
The International Space Station orbits 400 km above the Earth's surface. $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$; Earth: mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m.

**(a)** Calculate the gravitational field strength at this height. **[2]**

**(b)** Explain why astronauts on board feel weightless even though $g$ is not zero. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $g=\dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}$ with $r=6.77\times10^{6}$ m **(M1)**: $g=8.7\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$ **(A1)**

**(b)** The station and astronauts are in free fall together, accelerating at $g$; there is no normal contact force on the astronauts **(R1)**

prompt: Which statement about the gravitational field lines of an isolated planet is correct?
options: They point radially inwards and get further apart with distance.
They are evenly spaced at all distances.
markscheme: **B.** Field lines show the direction of force on a small mass: radially inwards. They are closer together near the planet, where the field is stronger; close to the surface over a small region they are approximately parallel (uniform field).

concept: Gravitational potential energy of a system
prompt: Explain why the gravitational potential energy of a satellite–Earth system is negative.
markscheme: $E_p$ is defined as the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation, where $E_p=0$ **(R1)**; gravity is attractive, so the field does positive work as the bodies come together and external work done is negative — energy must be supplied to separate them again **(R1)**

prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a 1000 kg satellite at a distance of $7.0\times10^{6}$ m from the Earth's centre. $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$; Earth: mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m.
What is the gravitational potential at the Earth's surface? (Earth mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m, $G=6.67\times10^{-11}$ SI units)
markscheme: **A.** $V_g=-\dfrac{GM}{R}=-6.3\times10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ — negative because the zero is at infinity.

prompt: Near the Earth's surface, $g=9.8\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$. Estimate the height difference between the equipotential surfaces $V_g=-62.5\ \text{MJ kg}^{-1}$ and $V_g=-62.4\ \text{MJ kg}^{-1}$.
markscheme: $|g|=\dfrac{\Delta V_g}{\Delta r}\Rightarrow\Delta r=\dfrac{0.1\times10^{6}}{9.8}$ **(M1)** $\approx1.0\times10^{4}$ m $=10$ km **(A1)** — the less negative surface is higher.

prompt: Calculate the minimum work needed to move a 1000 kg satellite from the Earth's surface to a distance of $7.0\times10^{6}$ m from the Earth's centre (ignoring its kinetic energy). $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$; Earth: mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m.
markscheme:
$V_1=-\dfrac{GM}{6.37\times10^{6}}=-6.25\times10^{7}$, $V_2=-\dfrac{GM}{7.0\times10^{6}}=-5.69\times10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ **(A1)**

$W=m\Delta V_g=1000\times5.6\times10^{6}$ **(M1)** $=5.6\times10^{9}$ J **(A1)**

Using $mg\Delta h$ would overestimate this, because $g$ falls with height.

prompt: How much work is done by the gravitational field when a mass moves along an equipotential surface?
markscheme: **A.** $W=m\Delta V_g$ and $\Delta V_g=0$ on an equipotential, so no work is done.

prompt: Describe the relationship between gravitational field lines and equipotential surfaces around a planet, and how the spacing of equipotentials for equal steps of $V_g$ changes with distance.
markscheme: Field lines are everywhere perpendicular to equipotential surfaces (concentric spheres) **(A1)**; for equal steps in $V_g$ the spheres get further apart with distance because the field (potential gradient) becomes weaker **(A1)**

prompt:
**(a)** Show that the escape speed from the Earth's surface is about $11\ \text{km s}^{-1}$. $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$; Earth: mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m. **[2]**

**(b)** Explain why the escape speed does not depend on the mass of the projectile. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $\tfrac12mv^{2}=\dfrac{GMm}{R}\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$ **(M1)** $=1.1\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ **(A1)**

**(b)** Both the kinetic energy and the potential energy needed are proportional to $m$, so it cancels **(R1)**

prompt:
$G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$; Earth: mass $5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.37\times10^{6}$ m.

**(a)** Calculate the orbital speed and period of a satellite 400 km above the surface. **[3]**

**(b)** Calculate the orbital radius of a geostationary satellite (period $8.62\times10^{4}$ s). **[2]**

concept: Effect of atmospheric drag on orbits
prompt: A satellite in a low orbit experiences a small drag force from the upper atmosphere. Explain what happens to its orbital radius and its speed.
markscheme:
Drag removes mechanical energy, so the total energy $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ becomes more negative and the radius decreases **(R1)**

$v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, so the speed **increases** as $r$ decreases **(A1)**; the loss of potential energy is twice the gain in kinetic energy, with the difference transferred to internal energy by drag **(R1)**
